name: Kero
material: Carved wood, often with painted scenes
powers: Twin cups shared to seal alliance and honor the sun.
description: The kero is the paired ceremonial drinking cup of the Andes, a flared goblet most often carved from wood, drunk from in twos at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. The paired cups were passed so that each party drank the other's offering, sealing friendship and reciprocal obligation, and the drink was usually chicha, the maize beer central to Andean ceremony. Inca nobles and officials received keros as marks of office, and the cups appear in colonial accounts as indispensable to the toasts that accompanied every treaty and celebration. After the Spanish conquest, colonial-era keros were painted with elaborate scenes of Inca life, rulers, animals and ceremony, creating a crucial record of how the empire remembered itself. The kero tradition survives among Andean communities, where the paired cup still seals the bonds of ayllu and fiesta.
source: Inca-period and colonial keros in museum collections

name: Tumi
powers: Sacrificial blade of the priests under the moon.
description: The tumi is the crescent-bladed ceremonial knife of the Andes, a wide arched blade of gold, silver, copper or bronze on a rectangular handle, used for sacrifices and depicted in Moche art cutting the throat of victims. Later Sican and Lambayeque metalworkers made ornate gold tumis crowned with the figure of Naylamp, the mythic founder of the Lambayeque dynasty shown as a bird-man, and the knife passed into Chimu and Inca ritual. The most famous example, the Tumi of Illimo or of Lambayeque, is a gold blade about 41 centimetres tall weighing nearly a kilogram, recovered from Huaca Las Ventanas at Batan Grande in 1936. Because most known examples are of precious metal, scholars believe they were largely symbolic, displayed in ritual and buried with lords rather than used for daily work. In modern Peru the tumi has become the national symbol of the country, reproduced in folk art, tourism souvenirs and even the emblem of the Peruvian College of Physicians.
source: Lambayeque/Sicán and Inca archaeological finds, including the Tumi of Lambayeque (1936)

name: Quipu
material: Colored and knotted cotton or camelid cords
era: Andean tradition to the colonial era
powers: Records numbers, tribute and histories in knots.
description: The quipu, or khipu, is the knotted-cord record-keeping system of the Andes, in which a main cord holds pendant cords whose colours, knot positions and spacings encode information, read by trained officials known as khipu-kamayuq. The Inca empire used quipus to keep accounts of tribute, census, harvests, armies, calendars and storerooms, and Spanish chroniclers called them the 'books' of the empire, records the colonial government could not match. Scholars have shown that the knots encode numbers in a decimal positional system, and a growing minority argues some quipus also carried narrative and genealogical meaning, though that reading remains debated. The cords were made of cotton or camelid fibre, and hundreds of examples survive, many unearthed from coastal tombs and highland caches. The Spanish destroyed thousands of quipus, yet some Andean communities continued to use them into the twentieth century, and the khipu has become a powerful symbol of Inca civilisation and of a knowledge system nearly lost.
source: Colonial chronicles and surviving Inca quipus

name: Mama Cocha Effigy
powers: Gains the protection of the mother of the sea.
description: Mama Cocha, the mother of the sea, was counted among the great Inca divinities, the wife and sister of the creator god Viracocha and the mother of Inti the sun and Mama Killa the moon. Fisherfolk along the Pacific coast made offerings of shells and small carved images, and poured maize beer into the waves, and colonial chroniclers record that the goddess was honored among the household and regional deities of the empire, receiving her share at the great festivals. Her image in miniature, worn as an amulet or set at the shore, carried her protection onto the boats that worked her waters, calming storms and guiding the catch. Though the Inca state collapsed, the cult of the sea mother survived in coastal communities, where she is sometimes said to ride the currents still and to reward the faithful with a full net. The effigies are the tangible trace of that devotion, small objects that held an ocean in the mind of an empire.
source: Colonial chronicles of Inca religion and coastal offerings

name: Pachamanca
material: Heated stones dug into the earth
powers: Feeds the community and returns its first taste to the earth.
description: The pachamanca is an Andean feast cooked in the earth: stones are heated in a dug pit, and layers of meat, potatoes, maize, beans and fragrant herbs are set over them, covered with leaves and earth, and steamed until done. The name comes from Quechua and means 'earth pot,' and the method is shared across the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands, where it is served at weddings, patronal fiestas, harvests and the raising of a new house. Before anyone eats, the first portion is set aside and offered to Pachamama, the earth mother, often with a splash of chicha or a libation poured on the ground, a gesture of return for what the land gave. Regional variants distinguish the cooking of the sierra from the coastal pachamanca a la olla, and the dish has become a badge of Andean identity even as families adapt it to modern stoves. The offering that opens the feast keeps alive the old understanding that eating from the earth demands giving back to it first.
source: Andean oral tradition and contemporary practice

name: Mate Gourd
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Shared in a circle that marks friendship and trust.
description: The mate gourd is the dried calabash cup from which yerba mate, the leafy infusion of the Guaraní, is drunk through a metal straw called a bombilla, passed hand to hand around a circle of friends. The Guaraní of Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina prepared a drink of the herb before the Spanish arrived, and colonial accounts already describe it being shared; the Spanish word mate itself comes from the Quechua mati, for the gourd that holds it. Etiquette is precise: the cebador pours, drinks the first, often bitter, sip and refills, and the gourd circles clockwise, never returning to the cebador for a second serving until it has passed everyone. To drink from another's gourd is an act of trust and closeness, which is why the sharing of mate is still the everyday gesture of friendship in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Modern gourds are carved and sometimes rimmed with metal, but the meaning is unchanged: one gourd, many hands, a shared breath.
source: Guaraní tradition and colonial accounts of mate

name: Bolas
material: Balls of stone or iron joined by braided hide cords
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Entangles the legs of running cattle or game.
description: The bolas, or boleadoras, are throwing weights of the South American plains: two or three stone or iron balls, often covered in hide, joined by braided cords of leather. The hunter or gaucho swings them overhead and releases them to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or rheas, tangling the animal in an instant fall. The weapon was developed by the Indigenous peoples of the Pampas and Patagonia and adopted wholesale by the colonial herders, and chroniclers recorded its use among the Mapuche and Tehuelche; a heavier solid type, the bolas perdidas, was hurled at enemies in war. The gaucho made the bolas his own, and the tool became so identified with him that it appears throughout the gauchesque literature, most famously in José Hernández's epic poem Martín Fierro. Today it survives in the cattle country of Argentina and Uruguay, used by the last horse-riding vaqueanos and kept alive as a symbol of the pampas.

name: Kultrún
powers: Carries the heartbeat of the land into ceremony.
description: The kultrún is the sacred drum of the Mapuche of Chile and Argentina, a shallow wooden bowl covered with a hide head and beaten with a single stick or by hand, played almost exclusively by the machi, the ritual specialist and healer. Its head is painted with a quartered design, a cross and the four directions, which orients the ceremony and maps the structure of the Mapuche universe, and around it the ngillatun ceremony of prayer and thanks is built. The machi sounds the kultrún to summon the spirits, to guide healing rites called machitun, and to call the community into a single rhythm; the drum is so closely tied to the office that a machi's calling is said to announce itself partly through the drum. The instrument is treated with the respect owed a sacred object, carried into the center of the ceremonial circle and held close by its keeper. In the twenty-first century the kultrún remains central to Mapuche religious life and has also become a symbol of Indigenous identity and resistance in Chile.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Rewe
material: Carved wooden post with notched steps
powers: Ladder by which the machi climbs to speak with the spirits.
description: The rewe is the carved altar pole of the Mapuche, a notched wooden post raised in the ceremonial ground and in front of the machi's home, its steps climbed by the machi during rituals to draw close to the upper world of the spirits. The notches are a ladder, and the rewe is understood as the axis linking the worlds, planted at the point where the sacred and the human meet; it is often topped with carved figures of the beings or animals that guide the machi. Each machi's rewe is raised with ceremony, receives offerings and chants, and marks the ritual space where the community gathers for the ngillatun, the great ceremony of thanks and petition. The rewe is so emblematic of the machi's office that it is read as the symbol of Mapuche spirituality, and contemporary Mapuche communities still erect and tend their rewes. It stands as a living sign that the sacred is not far away but planted in the very ground of the ceremonial field.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Saci's Red Cap
aliases: The Cap of the One-Legged Imp
era: Brazilian folk tradition to the present
powers: Whoever wins it gains the Saci's power.
description: The red cap of the Saci is the knitted head covering of the most famous figure of Brazilian folklore, the one-legged spirit Saci-Pererê, who smokes a pipe, whistles through the dark, and raises whirlwinds along the roads. The cap is the seat of his power, and the tales hold that whoever can catch him and take the cap wins the Saci's obedience or his magic, a prize that always slips away, because the trickster escapes as soon as the cap is grabbed. In some versions the color changes, with the red-capped Saci of the paths joined by variants wearing green or other colored caps, each with its own mischief. Monteiro Lobato's stories of the early twentieth century fixed the image of the pipe-smoking, red-capped trickster in the national imagination, though the figure long predates him in Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous legend. The cap alone identifies the Saci in folk art, carnival costumes and children's books, making it one of the most recognizable objects of Brazilian folk culture.
source: Brazilian oral tradition and Monteiro Lobato's tales

name: Supay Figurine
powers: Opens the door to the world beneath the earth.
description: Supay is the lord of the uku pacha, the world beneath the earth in Quechua cosmology, a realm of the dead and of the roots of the mountains; his images and masks, carved in stone or modeled in clay, stand for his power over that hidden country. In the colonial era his name was pressed into service as the Quechua word for the Christian devil, and the figure was forever blurred in two, ancient lord of the underworld on one side, Christian demon on the other. The ambiguity survives in the festivals of the Andes: at carnival and in the mining towns of Bolivia and Peru dancers wear elaborate Supay masks, and in the tin and silver mines he is courted with coca, cigarettes and chicha as the 'tío,' the uncle of the depths, who both gives the ore and may take the miner. Offerings and images of Supay were and are set out to keep his favor, especially by those who work beneath the earth. The figurine thus carries a double history, of the pre-Christian dead and of the devil the priests once taught.
source: Andean oral tradition and colonial records

name: Pishtaco Knife
era: Andean folk belief to the present
powers: Cuts fat from the living to sell it in secret.
description: The knife of the Pishtaco is the blade of the fat-stealer of the Andes, a figure who is said to creep upon sleeping travelers or the unwary on lonely roads and cut the fat from their bodies to sell it in secret, for candles, soap or, in the modern telling, to be shipped abroad for machines. The weapon is rarely seen; it is more feared than described, and a whistle or a shadow at the roadside is enough to raise the terror of the nakaq, as the same figure is called in Quechua. The belief is rooted in the real dread of the stranger and of the outsider, and historians note that it attached itself successively to Spanish priests, colonial officials, and later to police, missionaries and foreign aid workers, whichever authority the community distrusted. The knife is the visible edge of that fear, and stories of the Pishtaco circulate widely across Peru and Bolivia even today. It is one of the clearest cases in South American folklore of a weapon whose power lies not in its edge but in the story that hides behind it.
source: Andean folk belief and regional studies
